$$\mathcal R(\widehat r):=\check R\big((I-P)r^{-1}(\widehat r)\big)+R_P\big(Pr^{-1}(\widehat r)\big).$$

For $p\in[1,\infty)$, data $y^\delta\in Y$, and parameters $\alpha,\beta>0$, the **joint relaxed objective** is

$$\mathcal J_{\alpha,\beta}^\delta(\widehat r,x):=\|K\widehat r+F(x_0)-y^\delta\|_Y^p+\alpha\mathcal R(\widehat r)+\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p+\|Px\|_X^p,\qquad (\widehat r,x)\in\widetilde U\times U.$$

The joint source-condition objective takes $R_P=0$. The term $\beta Q(r(x),\widehat r)^p$ ties the relaxed range variable to the physical variable, while $\|Px\|_X^p$ penalizes the component outside $X_0$.

$$\partial R(x):=\{\xi\in X^*:R(z)\ge R(x)+\langle\xi,z-x\rangle_{X^*,X}\text{ for every }z\in X\}.$$

An element of $\partial R(x)$ is a subgradient of $R$ at $x$. Set $\partial R(x):=\varnothing$ when $x\notin\operatorname{dom}R$. The subdifferential may be empty at a point of $\operatorname{dom}R$; no nonemptiness assertion is part of this definition.

$$D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger):=R(x)-R(x^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}.$$

$$-\langle\xi^\dagger,x-x^\dagger\rangle_{X^*,X}\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(x,x^\dagger)+\psi\!\left(\|F(x)-F(x^\dagger)\|_Y^p\right)\qquad(x\in L_{R_0}).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$ and $\theta=1-1/p$, with
$W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$ as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]. Then the trace
operator $T$ of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] satisfies
$$\|Tu\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)} \qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)),$$
and it is onto: $T(W^{1,p}(\Omega))=W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$. For $p>1$
the range is a strict subset of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$, and the trace is not a
compact operator into $W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the boundary
conventions of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let
$0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix a
finite family of boundary charts: for each $j$ let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
be open and $\Phi_j:W_j\to\Phi_j(W_j)\subseteq B_j\times\mathbb R$ a
flattening chart as in
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], so that
$\Phi_j(\Omega\cap W_j)=\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t<0\}$ and the boundary corresponds
to the graph $\{t=0\}$; write $\Psi_j:=\pi\circ\Phi_j|_{\partial\Omega\cap W_j}$
for the induced parametrisation of $\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ by an open subset
$V_j:=\Psi_j(\partial\Omega\cap W_j)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and assume the
$\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ cover $\partial\Omega$. Fix a subordinate finite
ambient partition: nonnegative $\chi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\subseteq W_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a
neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega$
([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).
Finally let $\partial\Omega$ carry the chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], which fixes the
meaning of almost-everywhere equality and of $L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

For a Borel function $g:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb K$ put
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}:=\sum_j\bigl\|(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}\bigr\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})},$$
where the chart representation $(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}$ is read in graph
coordinates and extended by zero off $V_j$, and the norm on the right is that
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. The **fractional
Sobolev space of the boundary** is
$$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}<\infty\}.$$
The right-hand side is a finite sum of finite norms of compactly supported
chart representations, so $W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is exactly the
set of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ classes whose chart representations all lie in
the Euclidean space of
[[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]; that the resulting
space and the topology of the norm do not depend on the choices of atlas and
partition, up to equivalence of norms, is proved in
[[lem-fractional-boundary-norm-is-independent-of-atlas]] and is not assumed
here.

Three conventions belong to the definition. First, membership is a property of
the $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ class: $g$ is an almost-everywhere class with respect
to the surface measure, and the chart representations are classes in
$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$; representative independence for the Euclidean
factor is established together with the well-definedness lemma on this page
and is not presupposed here. Second, the norm is a finite sum
over a finite atlas, and each $\chi_jg$ is supported in the interior of the
chart, so the localisations are compactly supported and no boundary behaviour
of $\Psi_j^{-1}$ outside $V_j$ enters. Third, on this page the exponent used
is the trace exponent $s=\theta=1-1/p$ for $1<p<\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $u-v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, then [F2] gives $Tu=Tv$, so $\overline T[u]:=Tu$ is well-defined on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$. By [F1], $\|\overline T[u]\|_{W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$ for every representative $u$; taking the infimum over its coset gives $\|\overline T[u]\|\le C\|[u]\|_{\mathcal D}$. If $\overline T[u]=0$, [F2] gives $u\in H_0^1$, hence $[u]=0$; thus the induced map is injective.

By [F1], every $f\in W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ is $Tu$ for some $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, so $\overline T$ is onto. More quantitatively, choose the lift $Rf$ from [F3]. Then $\overline T[Rf]=f$ and $\|[Rf]\|_{\mathcal D}\le\|Rf\|_{H^1}\le C\|f\|_{W^{1/2,2}}$, proving that the inverse is bounded.

The trace of a constant function is that same constant, so $\overline T$ maps the closed constant subspace $\mathbb K\mathbf1\subset\mathcal D(\Omega)$ onto the constant subspace of $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$. The bounded isomorphism and its bounded inverse from steps 1.1–1.2 therefore induce a bounded isomorphism on the two quotient spaces, with equivalent quotient norms.

If $\ell$ is a continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ that annihilates constants, then $\dot\ell([f]):=\ell(f)$ is independent of the representative because $\ell(f+c)=\ell(f)$ for every constant $c$. By the quotient-norm definition, $|\dot\ell([f])|\le\|\ell\|\inf_c\|f+c\|_{W^{1/2,2}}$, so $\dot\ell$ is continuous with quotient dual norm at most $\|\ell\|$. Conversely, any functional that factors as $\ell=\varphi\circ q$ vanishes on constants because $q(c)=0$; and $|\varphi(qf)|\le\|\varphi\|\|qf\|\le\|\varphi\|\|f\|$ because the quotient map $q$ has norm at most one. Hence $\|\ell\|\le\|\varphi\|$, while the first inequality gives $\|\varphi\|\le\|\ell\|$ for the induced functional. This proves the equivalence and equality of dual norms.

For every $\ell\ge0$, $\dim_\mathbb C\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$; the spaces $\mathcal H_\ell$ are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$ and their algebraic sum is dense there. Thus they give a complete orthogonal spherical-harmonic expansion. For any orthonormal basis $Y_{\ell 1},\ldots,Y_{\ell,2\ell+1}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$, the basis-independent reproducing kernel
$$Z_\ell(\omega,\eta):=\sum_{m=1}^{2\ell+1}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\eta)}$$
satisfies $Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. In particular,
$$|g(\omega)|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_{L^2(S^2)}\qquad(g\in\mathcal H_\ell).$$
For fixed $\eta$, rotational invariance makes $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$ a degree-$\ell$ zonal polynomial of $\omega\cdot\eta$; normalizing $P_\ell(1)=1$ gives the usual addition identity $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\eta)$.

$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero

The induced map after quotienting by constants is also a bounded linear bijection $\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb K\mathbf1\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)/\mathbb K$, with equivalent quotient norms. A continuous linear functional on $W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ descends to the constant quotient exactly when it annihilates constants, and its descended functional has the quotient dual norm.

The divergence theorem [F5] gives the Green identity for smooth approximants; density [F6] and trace continuity [F4] pass it to the $H^2$ CGO solutions on $B_1$. On the collar $U_j$ is harmonic and the coefficient is identically one. Taking the test function one shows $\int f_j=0$. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}u_j=\mathscr N_j f_j+c_j$ for a constant $c_j$.

Subtract the two bilinear Schrödinger Green identities [F5]–[F6], testing the $j=1$ equation against $U_2$ and the $j=2$ equation against $U_1$. Their gradient terms cancel, giving $\int Q U_1U_2=\int_{S^2}(f_1\operatorname{Tr}U_2-f_2\operatorname{Tr}U_1)$. Since $U_j=u_j$ on the boundary, step 2.1 identifies these traces with $\mathscr N_jf_j+c_j$. The constant terms disappear because the fluxes have mean zero; the symmetry from step 1.1 gives exactly the displayed centered NtD identity. All volume terms are integrable since $Q\in L^2$ and $U_j\in H^2(B_2)\subset L^\infty(B_1)$; boundedness follows, for example, by weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz after multiplication by an interior cutoff.

If $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$, [F3] and differentiation of the exponential give $\|U_j\|_{H^2(B_1)}\le Ce^{Ct}t^3$ for $t\ge T$. For smooth compactly supported $w$ put $[w]^2_{1/2}:=\iint|w(x)-w(y)|^2|x-y|^{-4}\,dx\,dy$. Translation, Plancherel and Tonelli [F7] give $$[w]^2_{1/2}=\int|\widehat w(\xi)|^2\left(\int\frac{|e^{i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2}{|h|^4}\,dh\right)d\xi=c_3\int|\xi||\widehat w(\xi)|^2d\xi,$$ where rotation and dilation give the inner integral, and $0<c_3<\infty$ follows from $|e^{iu}-1|\le\min\{2,|u|\}$. Thus $\|w\|_{H^{1/2}}^2\asymp\|w\|_2^2+[w]^2_{1/2}$. Restrict each $H^2(B_2)$ remainder to $B_1$ and use [F6] to approximate it there by ambient smooth functions; multiplication by a cutoff supported in $B_1$ and [F8] extend the products to $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, so the norm comparison extends to these cutoff remainders. For bounded compactly supported factors the identity $f(x)g(x)-f(y)g(y)=f(x)(g(x)-g(y))+g(y)(f(x)-f(y))$ then yields $\|fg\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C(\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}+\|g\|_\infty\|f\|_{H^{1/2}})$. Applying the product estimate to $\chi r_j$ and $\eta r_j$, and [F3], gives $\|\chi(r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)\|_{H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^3)}\le C/t$. This proves the stated estimate with its modulation factor retained.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Put $\Omega=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$, fix $0<\rho<1$, and let $5/2<s<7/2$ and $s<t<2s-1$. Use the following precise intrinsic Hilbert norm on $H^s(\Omega)$. If $s=m+\theta$ with integer $m\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$, set
$$\|v\|_{s,\Omega}^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\|D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\Omega\times\Omega}\frac{|D^\alpha v(x)-D^\alpha v(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{3+2\theta}}\,dx\,dy.$$
For integer $s=3$ use just the derivative sum with $m=3$. Denote the corresponding real inner product by $(\cdot,\cdot)_{s,\Omega}$. On $\mathbb R^3$ use the unitary Fourier transform and $\|f\|_{H^r}^2=\int\langle\xi\rangle^{2r}|\widehat f(\xi)|^2d\xi$. Let $B^r_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ have norm $\sup_{j\ge0}2^{jr}\|\mathbf1_{A_j}\widehat f\|_2$, where $A_0=\{|\xi|<2\}$ and $A_j=\{2^j\le|\xi|<2^{j+1}\}$ for $j\ge1$; the restriction space on $\Omega$ consists of restrictions of members of this whole-space Besov space.

Let $\sigma^\dagger\in H^s(\Omega)\cap B^t_{2,\infty}(\Omega)$ be real and equal to $1$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus B_\rho$. Then there is $C>0$, depending on $\sigma^\dagger,s,t,\rho$, such that for every real $\sigma\in H^s(\Omega)$ also equal to $1$ there and every integer $J\ge0$,
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le C2^{J(2s-t-1)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-J(t-s)}\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}.$$
Consequently, suppose on a specified admissible sublevel a forward map $G$ satisfies $\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_0\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$ with $\omega(0)=0$ and $0\le\omega\le1$. For the exact regularizer $R(\sigma)=\frac12\|\sigma\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, its exact Bregman distance is $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\frac12\|\sigma-\sigma^\dagger\|_{s,\Omega}^2$, and
$$-(\sigma^\dagger,\sigma-\sigma^\dagger)_{s,\Omega}\le\frac34D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)+C_1\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)^{2(t-s)/(t-1)}.$$
In particular, an $H^1$ stability modulus of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-(s-3/2)}$ yields a VSC source term of order $[\log(1/u)]^{-\nu}$ with $\nu=(t-s)(2s-3)/(t-1)$. The conditional stability estimate is a hypothesis here, not a conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Suppose
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact
set $K_0\subset\Omega$. Let $E_0u$ denote the extension of a representative of
$u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$, and for $|\alpha|\le k$ let
$E_0(D^\alpha u)$ denote the extension by zero of the corresponding
derivative representative. Then
$$E_0u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad D^\alpha(E_0u)=E_0(D^\alpha u)\quad\text{almost everywhere, }|\alpha|\le k,$$
and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0(D^\alpha u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. The case
$k=0$ is included, and complex scalars are handled by the same bilinear
pairing.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

An **$L^1$ approximate identity** on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a family
$(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where

$$\|K_\varepsilon\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx,$$

such that:

1. $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} K_\varepsilon(x)\,dx = 1$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$;
2. there is $M < \infty$ with $\|K_\varepsilon\|_1 \le M$ for every
   $\varepsilon > 0$;
3. for every $\delta > 0$,
   $$ \int_{|x|>\delta} |K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+). $$

This is the general notion used later for both compactly supported mollifiers
and the Gaussian family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|a\|_\infty+\|\nabla a\|_\infty\le C_s\|a\|_{H^s}$ because $\int(1+|\xi|^2)^{-s}(1+|\xi|)^2d\xi<\infty$ for $s>5/2$. The Fourier integrals for $a$ and its first derivatives converge absolutely and are continuous by dominated convergence, so these bounds hold for a $C^1$ representative. We shall also use $\|fg\|_{H^b}\le C\|f\|_{H^r}\|g\|_{H^b}$ when $r>3/2$ and $0\le b\le r$. Here is a direct justification: split Fourier space into dyadic annuli, use $\|f_j\|_\infty\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_j\|_2$ for low-high products, and $\|Q_j(f_kg_k)\|_2\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_k\|_2\|g_k\|_2$ when comparable high shells $k$ produce a shell $j\le k+C$. For high-low products, sum the low $g$ blocks with bound $C2^{j(3/2-b)}\|g\|_{H^b}$ if $b<3/2$, a square-root logarithmic factor if $b=3/2$, or $C\|g\|_{H^b}$ if $b>3/2$; the excess $r-3/2>0$ makes the resulting geometric sum converge. For high-high products, weighted summation over $k\ge j-C$ has geometric kernel $2^{-(k-j)(r+b)}$ and excess factor $2^{j(3/2-r)}$; Cauchy–Schwarz for the input shell sequences completes the bound. The estimates are first proved for Fourier truncations and then passed to their norm limits.

For $0<\theta<1$, multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function $h$ is bounded on $H^\theta$. Indeed $|h(x)f(x)-h(y)f(y)|^2\le2\|h\|_\infty^2|f(x)-f(y)|^2+2|f(y)|^2|h(x)-h(y)|^2$. In the last term use $|h(x)-h(y)|\le\min\{2\|h\|_\infty,\|\nabla h\|_\infty|x-y|\}$; integrating the kernel $|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}$ near and far from the diagonal gives a finite constant times $\|f\|_2^2$. Apply [F2] to get the Fourier Sobolev bound. For $\theta=0$ this is just the $L^2$ multiplier bound.

If $F$ is any smooth scalar function on a neighborhood of $[m,M]$, then $F(1+a)-F(1)$ belongs to $H^s$ with a uniform bound over this class. To verify the fractional highest derivative directly, write $s=k+\theta$ with $k=2$ or $3$ and $0\le\theta<1$. For $k=2$, the chain rule gives terms $F'(\sigma)D^2a$ and $F''(\sigma)Da\,Da$. The first term is in $H^\theta$ by step 2.1, since $F'(\sigma)$ is bounded $C^1$ uniformly; for the second, $Da\in H^{s-1}$ with $s-1>3/2$, so the algebra bound in step 1.1 and then step 2.1 apply. For $k=3$, the terms are $F'(\sigma)D^3a$, $F''(\sigma)D^2a\,Da$, and $F'''(\sigma)(Da)^3$. Here $Da\in H^{s-1}$ is a multiplier on $H^{s-2}$ by step 1.1, so $D^2a\,Da\in H^{s-2}\subset H^\theta$; the remaining products follow from the same algebra and step 2.1. Lower derivatives have the corresponding easier estimates; the function itself has an $L^2$ bound by the mean value theorem and vanishes wherever $a=0$. These calculations may first be made for smooth approximations: convolve $a$ with a nonnegative mollifier, which preserves $m\le1+a\le M$ and uniform $H^s$ and $C^1$ bounds, and then use convergence in lower Sobolev orders and weak compactness in the Hilbert $H^s$ space to identify the asserted weak derivatives and bound. A bounded sequence in this separable Fourier Hilbert space has a weakly convergent subsequence by diagonal convergence of its countable Fourier coordinates and the norm bound; hence only Countable Choice is used.

Apply step 3.1 to $F(t)=\sqrt t$, $\frac12\log t$, and $t^{-1/2}$ to obtain the stated regularity and support of $g_j-1$, $\log g_j$, and $g_j^{-1}-1$. To bound $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ in $H^{s-2}$, for $s<3$ use step 2.1 with $\theta=s-2\in(1/2,1)$ and the uniform $C^1$ norm of $g_j^{-1}$; for $s\ge3$ use the multiplier bound in step 1.1 with $r=s$ and $b=s-2$. Split $g_j^{-1}=1+(g_j^{-1}-1)$ for that whole-space bound. The support statement follows from $g_j=1$ outside the collar ball and from the local definition of weak derivatives.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$, $H=g_1g_2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$. Since $H
abla w=g_2
abla g_1-g_1
abla g_2$, distributional differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)=g_2\Delta g_1-g_1\Delta g_2=HQ$. The equality follows first for smooth positive approximations and then in distributions using step 4.1 and the Sobolev products from steps 1.1–2.1; all terms also have their ordinary weak-product interpretation because $g_j$ are $C^1$ and $\Delta g_j\in L^2$. The functions $w$ and its gradient vanish outside $\overline{B_ho}$. By [F3], extend $w$ by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. Choose a nonnegative unit-mass smooth mollifier from [F4]. For small $\varepsilon$, its convolution with the zero extension is supported in $B_2$; by [F5], the mollifications converge to $w$ in $H^1$. Thus the distributional identity may be tested against $w$: $Q\in H^{-1}$ and multiplication by the bounded $C^1$ function $H$ is bounded on $H^1$. It gives $\int H|
abla w|^2=-\langle Q,Hwangle$.

A compactly supported $H^1$ function in $B_\rho\subset(-2,2)^3$ obeys $\|w\|_2\le4\|\partial_1w\|_2$: for a smooth approximation supported in the same larger cube, write $w(x_1,x')=\int_{-2}^{x_1}\partial_1w(t,x')dt$, apply Cauchy–Schwarz, and integrate in $x_1,x'$; passing to $H^1$ limits gives the inequality. Since $H\ge m$, step 5.1 and the Fourier dual bound yield $m\|\nabla w\|_2^2\le\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\|Hw\|_{H^1}\le C\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\|w\|_{H^1}$. Poincaré in the first sentence then implies $\|w\|_{H^1}\le C\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}$, dividing by its norm if nonzero. Finally $\sigma_1-\sigma_2=\sigma_2(e^{2w}-1)$; the uniform bounds for $w$, $\sigma_2$ and $\nabla\sigma_2$, the mean value theorem, and the ordinary weak product rule give $\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1}\le C\|w\|_{H^1}$. Also $\|Q\|_{H^{-1}}\le\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ by the Fourier weights. This proves all recovery claims.

$$\|U\|_{H^s}=\bigl\|\langle\xi\rangle^s\mathcal F(E_sU)\bigr\|_2$$

convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: We record explicitly the smooth-multiplication bound for the stated Besov convention. Write $Q_j=\mathbf1_{A_j}(D)$. For $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $Q_j\chi Q_k$ has Fourier kernel $(2\pi)^{-3/2}\mathbf1_{A_j}(\xi)\widehat\chi(\xi-\eta)\mathbf1_{A_k}(\eta)$. If $|j-k|\le2$, Young's convolution inequality [F3] bounds its $L^2$ operator norm by a constant times $\|\widehat\chi\|_1$. If $|j-k|>2$, then $|\xi-\eta|\ge c2^{\max(j,k)}$ on these supports. Repeated integration by parts in the Fourier integral of $\chi$ gives $|\widehat\chi(\zeta)|\le C_N(1+|\zeta|)^{-N}$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the two frequency variables therefore bounds the operator norm by $C_N2^{-N\max(j,k)}2^{3(j+k)/2}$. For any real $r$, multiply these bounds by $2^{jr-kr}$ and sum over $k$. Choosing $N>2|r|+8$ makes both off-diagonal geometric sums uniformly bounded in $j$, while the near-diagonal sum has at most five terms. Hence $\|\chi f\|_{B^r_{2,\infty}}\le C_{r,\chi}\|f\|_{B^r_{2,\infty}}$. These calculations first apply to finite block sums; the same estimates give their convergence in distributions, since a Schwartz test has faster-than-polynomial Fourier decay.

The sharp annular definition agrees, up to constants, with any usual smooth inhomogeneous dyadic definition at $p=2$. Indeed a sharp annulus meets at most a fixed number of the smooth supports at neighboring scales. On that annulus, the identity $\sum\varphi_j=1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give its $L^2$ norm at most the sum of those finitely many smooth-block $L^2$ norms; conversely each smooth symbol has magnitude at most one and support in finitely many sharp annuli. The weights $2^{jr}$ differ by only a constant at neighboring scales. The low blocks also meet only finitely many supports. This proves both Besov norm comparisons. For Hilbert Sobolev norms, [F1] gives directly $\|f\|_{H^r}^2\asymp\sum_j2^{2jr}\|Q_jf\|_2^2$, consistently with [F2].

Choose $\chi_0\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one near $\overline{B_\rho}$, and choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ equal to one near $\overline\Omega$. Let $\widetilde\sigma^\dagger$ be one whole-space $B^t_{2,\infty}$ extension, whose existence is part of the restriction-space hypothesis. The compactly supported distribution $f^\dagger:=\chi_0(\widetilde\sigma^\dagger-1)$ is in $B^t_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3)$ by step 1.1 (the constant term multiplied by $\chi_0$ is smooth). It equals $\sigma^\dagger-1$ on $\Omega$ and vanishes outside $\overline{B_\rho}$, since the conductivity equals one in the collar. Thus $v^\dagger=\eta+f^\dagger$ is a compactly supported $B^t_{2,\infty}$ extension of $\sigma^\dagger$. In particular $v^\dagger\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$: the squared block sum is bounded by a constant times $\sum_j2^{-2j(t-s)}<\infty$.

For $e=\sigma-\sigma^\dagger$, let $e_0$ be its zero extension. Its support lies in $\overline{B_\rho}$. Zero extension creates no boundary derivatives because $e$ vanishes on an open collar: local distributional tests near $\partial\Omega$ see zero, and interior tests give exactly the zero extensions of the weak derivatives. For $s=m+\theta$ noninteger, the whole-space top-order difference integral equals the integral over $\Omega^2$ plus $2\int_\Omega|D^\alpha e(x)|^2\int_{\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega}|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy\,dx$. Where $D^\alpha e$ can be nonzero, the inner integral is bounded by $\int_{|z|\ge1-\rho}|z|^{-3-2\theta}dz<\infty$. The whole-space difference norm is therefore bounded by $C\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, and the integer case is immediate. For $g\in L^2$, [F1] and Tonelli [F4] give $\int\int|g(x+h)-g(x)|^2|h|^{-3-2\theta}dx\,dh=\int|\widehat g(\xi)|^2\int|e^{i\xi\cdot h}-1|^2|h|^{-3-2\theta}dh\,d\xi$. The inner integral equals $c_\theta|\xi|^{2\theta}$ by rotation and dilation; $0<c_\theta<\infty$ follows by the bounds $|e^{iu}-1|\le\min\{2,|u|\}$. Summing derivative multipliers shows that this whole-space difference norm is equivalent to $\|e_0\|_{H^s}$. Thus $\|e_0\|_{H^s}\le C\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, while exactly $\|e_0\|_{H^1}=\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$.

Let $B_s(v,w)$ be the whole-space intrinsic bilinear form associated with the derivative and difference norm in step 3.2. Its Fourier multiplier $p_s(\xi)$ equals $\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\xi^{2\alpha}+c_\theta\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\xi^{2\alpha}|\xi|^{2\theta}$ in the noninteger case, and just the first polynomial in the integer case. Thus $|p_s(\xi)|\le C\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}$, and $P_0:=p_s(D)v^\dagger$ belongs to $B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$ by the annular multiplier bound and step 3.1. Its distributional pairing with $e_0$ is $B_s(v^\dagger,e_0)$. The pairing is defined by convergent Fourier blocks: high blocks have the product bound $C2^{-j(t-s)}\|e_0\|_{H^s}$, a summable sequence. This also justifies the bilinear identity by truncation and limits, without assuming classical derivatives of order $2s$.

In the integer case the whole-space and domain pairings are identical, since every derivative of $e_0$ is supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$; take $P=P_0$. For noninteger $s=m+\theta$, their difference is $$B_s(v^\dagger,e_0)-(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}=2\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_\Omega D^\alpha e(x)\big(A(x)D^\alpha v^\dagger(x)-b_\alpha(x)\big)dx,$$ where $A(x)=\int_{\Omega^c}|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy$ and $b_\alpha(x)=\int_{\Omega^c}D^\alpha\eta(y)|x-y|^{-3-2\theta}dy$. To obtain the formula, split each whole-space double integral into $\Omega^2$, $\Omega\times\Omega^c$ and its transpose; $D^\alpha e_0$ is zero outside and $v^\dagger=\eta$ there. On any fixed neighborhood of $\overline{B_\rho}$ compact in $\Omega$, every derivative of $A,b_\alpha$ is bounded, by differentiating the separated kernel and using its integrable tail. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one on that neighborhood. The domain pairing is therefore the pairing of $e_0$ with $$P=P_0-2\sum_{|\alpha|=m}(-1)^mD^\alpha\big(\chi A D^\alpha v^\dagger-\chi b_\alpha\big).$$ By step 1.1, its correction terms lie in $B^{t-2m}_{2,\infty}$: differentiation lowers the block regularity by the derivative order, multiplication by the smooth compact coefficient preserves it, and $\chi b_\alpha$ is smooth and compactly supported. Since $2m\le2s$, they also lie in $B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$. Hence $P\in B^{t-2s}_{2,\infty}$ in every case, and $\langle P,e_0\rangle=(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}$. This treats the exact domain penalty pairing rather than replacing its norm by an equivalent one.

Put $d=t-s>0$ and $a=2s-t-1>0$. Let $P_{\le J}=\sum_{j\le J}Q_jP$. By step 5.1 and the Hilbert block norm formula, $\|P_{\le J}\|_{H^{-1}}^2\le C\sum_{j\le J}2^{2j(2s-t-1)}\le C2^{2Ja}$. Similarly $\|P-P_{\le J}\|_{H^{-s}}^2\le C\sum_{j>J}2^{2j(s-t)}\le C2^{-2Jd}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz and step 3.2 now give $|\langle P,e_0\rangle|\le C2^{Ja}\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}+C2^{-Jd}\|e\|_{s,\Omega}$, the first claimed estimate.

Expansion of the quadratic form gives exactly $D_R(\sigma,\sigma^\dagger)=\|e\|_{s,\Omega}^2/2$. Set $W=\omega(\|G(\sigma)-G(\sigma^\dagger)\|)$. The conditional stability hypothesis and $uv\le3u^2/8+2v^2/3$ applied to the high-frequency term in step 6.1 yield $-(\sigma^\dagger,e)_{s,\Omega}\le3\|e\|_{s,\Omega}^2/8+C(2^{Ja}W+2^{-2Jd})$. Since $a+2d=t-1$, this proves the asserted source inequality with coefficient $3/4$ on the exact Bregman distance. Substitution of the stated logarithmic stability exponent gives $\nu=2(s-3/2)(t-s)/(t-1)$ by multiplying exponents.

Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$

Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Choose a smooth scalar function $\vartheta$ with $0\le\vartheta\le1$, equal to one on $[m,M]$ and zero outside $(m/2,2M)$, and set $g(t)=1+\int_1^t\vartheta(u)du$. Since $\sigma_0+a=1$ outside $B_\rho$ and $g(1)=1$, $b(a)\in E$ for every $a\in V$. Moreover, $a\mapsto b(a)$ is globally Lipschitz from $V$ into $E$ and continuously Fréchet differentiable, with derivative $b'(a)h=g'(\sigma_0+a)h$ and globally Lipschitz derivative; its Taylor remainder is bounded by $\frac12\|g''\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty^2$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: We give the Sobolev product bounds used below. They hold for periodic functions on a fixed three-dimensional cube, and for the product of a periodic function and a function with one fixed half-integer Fourier shift. The constants can be chosen uniformly under rotations of the cube. Split Fourier frequencies into dyadic shells and write $f_j,g_j$ for the corresponding blocks. A shell contains at most $C2^{3j}$ lattice points, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|f_j\|_\infty\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_j\|_2$. For $r>3/2$ and $0\le s\le r$, these estimates prove $\|fg\|_{H^s}\le C\|f\|_{H^r}\|g\|_{H^s}$. For low $f$ against high $g$, use $\|f_{<j-2}\|_\infty\le C\|f\|_{H^r}$ and square-sum $2^{js}\|g_j\|_2$. For high $f$ against low $g$, when $s<3/2$ use $\|g_{<j-2}\|_\infty\le C2^{j(3/2-s)}\|g\|_{H^s}$, and when $s>3/2$ use the uniform bound by $\|g\|_{H^s}$; the critical case has an extra factor $(1+j)^{1/2}$, absorbed by $2^{-j(r-3/2)}$. The resulting weighted terms are bounded by $2^{-j(r-3/2)}\|f\|_{H^r}\|g\|_{H^s}$ or by $2^{js}\|f_j\|_2\|g\|_{H^s}$. For comparable high input shells $k$ that produce an output shell $j\le k+C$, use $\|Q_j(f_kg_k)\|_2\le C2^{3j/2}\|f_k\|_2\|g_k\|_2$, obtained from the $L^1$ bound on the product and the number of output frequencies. Multiplication by $2^{js}$ and summation over $k\ge j-C$ gives a summable geometric kernel, since $r+s>0$ and $r>3/2$; at $s=r=0$ this case is not being used. Cauchy–Schwarz for the two input shell sequences and the geometric kernel completes the $H^s$ bound.

Rotate so that $\zeta=s(e_1+ie_2)$, where $s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$, and choose a fixed cube $Q=(-\pi L,\pi L)^3$ containing $\overline{B_3}$. Put $\eta_k=(k+e_2/2)/L$ and use the shifted orthonormal basis $w_k=(2\pi L)^{-3/2}e^{i\eta_k\cdot x}$. For $A_\zeta=D^2+2\zeta\cdot D$, $D=-i\nabla$, its symbol is $p_k=|\eta_k|^2+2\zeta\cdot\eta_k$, with $|\operatorname{Im}p_k|\ge s/L$. For $|\eta_k|\le4s$, this gives $|p_k|\ge s/L$; for $|\eta_k|>4s$, its real part has magnitude at least $|\eta_k|^2/2$. Hence for every real $\mu$ and $0\le v\le2$ the coefficient multiplier $G_\zeta:p_k^{-1}$ satisfies $\|G_\zeta f\|_{H^{\mu+v}(Q)}\le C_v s^{v-1}\|f\|_{H^\mu(Q)}$ for $s\ge1$. The Sobolev spaces here are defined by the shifted weighted coefficient norms. Parseval proves these bounds and $A_\zeta G_\zeta f=f$ in distributions inside $Q$, first on finite sums and then by convergence.

A second bound is $\|fg\|_{H^{-1/2}}\le C_\varepsilon\|f\|_{H^{1/2+\varepsilon}}\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$ for every $0<\varepsilon<1$. Here the low-high and high-low estimates from step 1.1, with output weight $2^{-j/2}$, have the additional decay $2^{-\varepsilon j}$. For comparable high shells, the output estimate becomes $2^j\sum_{k\ge j-C}\|f_k\|_2\|g_k\|_2=2^{-\varepsilon j}\sum_{k\ge j-C}2^{-(k-j)(1+\varepsilon)}F_kG_k$, with $F_k=2^{k(1/2+\varepsilon)}\|f_k\|_2$ and $G_k=2^{k/2}\|g_k\|_2$. The geometric kernel has finite sum, and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the product sequence in $\ell^1$ by $\|F\|_2\|G\|_2$. This proves the claimed bound. All product calculations first hold for finite Fourier sums; the bounds give convergence in the target Sobolev space and identify the product as the distributional limit. Whenever one factor belongs to $H^r$, $r>3/2$, its Fourier coefficients are absolutely summable by weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, so it is a bounded continuous multiplier and this distributional product agrees with the ordinary product.

The periodic and shifted Sobolev norms of the compactly supported potential are bounded by $C\|q\|_{H^{1/2+\tau}(\mathbb R^3)}\le CM$. For completeness, choose a fixed smooth cutoff equal to one on $B_1$ and supported in $B_2$. Since it multiplies $q$ without changing it, each Fourier coefficient of $q$ is the convolution of its whole-space Fourier transform with a translate of the rapidly decreasing transform of this cutoff, sampled at an integer or shifted lattice point. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, followed by summation over the lattice, bounds the coefficient norm by the whole-space norm: the sums $\sup_\xi\sum_k(1+|\eta_k-\xi|)^{-N}$ and the corresponding integrals are finite for $N>3$, and polynomial Sobolev weights are absorbed by increasing $N$. The reverse local bound needed later follows in the same way by multiplying the Fourier series by a smooth cutoff supported inside $Q$ and equal to one on $B_2$, then estimating the resulting convolution sum in whole-space weighted $L^2$. The cutoffs can be chosen radial before rotation, so all constants are independent of the phase direction.

Put $r_0=3/2+\tau/2$ and $h_0=r_0-1=1/2+\tau/2$. Split the periodic potential into $q=q_\sharp+q_\flat$ by retaining frequencies of size at most $2^J$ in $q_\sharp$. Then $\|q_\flat\|_{H^{h_0}}\le C2^{-J\tau/2}M$, whereas $q_\sharp$ has bounded Sobolev norms of every order with bounds depending only on $J,M$. Choose $J$, depending only on $\tau,M$, so that $G_\zeta q_\flat$ as a multiplication-composition operator has norm at most $1/4$ both on shifted $H^{r_0}$ and on shifted $H^{1/2}$. On $H^{r_0}$ this follows from the product bound in step 1.1, with multiplier $r\in H^{r_0}$ and $q_\flat\in H^{h_0}$, and the $v=1$ bound of step 1.2. On $H^{1/2}$ it follows from step 2.1 with $\varepsilon=\tau/2$ and the same $v=1$ bound. Next choose $s$ large enough, depending only on $J,M,\tau$, that $G_\zeta q_\sharp$ has norm at most $1/4$ on both spaces, using the smooth multiplier bound from step 1.1 and the $v=0$ bound $C/s$ from step 1.2. Thus $I+G_\zeta q$ has inverse given by a convergent geometric series, of norm at most two, on both spaces.

Define $r_\zeta=-(I+G_\zeta q)^{-1}G_\zeta q$ in shifted $H^{r_0}$. The forcing $q$ in the last position is the actual compactly supported function on $Q$, represented in the shifted basis; the multiplication operators use the periodic representation of the same function. These agree pointwise inside $Q$. Step 1.2 with $\mu=1/2+\tau$ and $v=1-\tau/2$ gives $\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{r_0}(Q)}\le Cs^{-\tau/2}M$. Since $r_0>3/2$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz for its coefficients gives $\|r_\zeta\|_\infty\le C\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{r_0}(Q)}$. This solution is also the unique shifted $H^{1/2}$ solution, by the second invertibility statement in step 3.1; using step 1.2 with $\mu=1/2,v=0$ gives $\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{1/2}(Q)}\le Cs^{-1}M$. Finally, its equation is $r_\zeta=-G_\zeta(q+qr_\zeta)$; since $q\in L^2$ and $r_\zeta\in L^\infty$, the $v=2$ bound from $L^2$ gives $\|r_\zeta\|_{H^2(Q)}\le CsM(1+M)$, enlarging the threshold to keep $s\ge1$.

Applying $A_\zeta$ to the equation in step 4.1 gives $A_\zeta r_\zeta+q(1+r_\zeta)=0$ in the interior of $Q$. Direct conjugation and $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ show this is exactly $(-\Delta+q)(e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta))=0$. The local comparison in step 2.2 transfers the fractional bounds to restriction norms on $B_2$, and restriction gives the integer $H^2$ bound there. Pulling back the initial rotation preserves the whole-space potential norm, the support ball, and the Euclidean PDE. Since $s=|\zeta|/\sqrt2$, step 4.1 yields all displayed estimates. The construction was on a fixed larger cube, so it imposes no boundary condition on the unit ball and supplies regularity on its full neighborhood.

Suppose $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $a_j$ is real, supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^3)}\le A$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for $j=1,2$. Then $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$ and $\log g_j$ belong to $C^1$, with $g_j-1,\log g_j\in H^s(\mathbb R^3)$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$ and uniformly bounded in $H^s$ and $C^1$. The real Liouville potentials
$$q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$$
belong to $H^{s-2}(\mathbb R^3)$, have support in $\overline{B_\rho}$, and have norms bounded in terms of $s,\rho,m,M,A$. Moreover,
$$\|\sigma_1-\sigma_2\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1}(\mathbb R^3)},$$
with the same dependence. In particular the right side may be replaced by $C\|q_1-q_2\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ when that stronger norm is used. The Fourier and intrinsic norms for collared variations are those of the collared Sobolev source-functional lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\Omega=B_1\subset\mathbb R^3$, and let $\sigma_j=1+a_j$ be positive real conductivities with $a_j$ supported in $\overline{B_\rho}$, $\|a_j\|_{H^s}\le A$, $5/2<s<7/2$, $0<\rho<1$, and $m\le\sigma_j\le M$, for fixed positive bounds. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\sigma_j}$, $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$, $Q=q_1-q_2$, and $N=\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}(\mathbb R^3)}$. Let $\mathscr N_j$ be the boundary-mean-zero Neumann-to-Dirichlet map for $\sigma_j$ on $L^2_0(S^2)$, and define the actual data difference by the centered voltage sequences
$$\delta=\left(\sum_{\ell\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{2\ell+1}\|(\mathscr N_1-\mathscr N_2)Y_{\ell k}\|_{L^2(S^2)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
This quantity is finite. If $U_j=e^{i\zeta_j\cdot x}(1+r_j)$ are the solutions from the positive-Sobolev CGO lemma, then
$$\int_\Omega Q U_1U_2\,dx=\int_{S^2}f_1(\mathscr N_2-\mathscr N_1)f_2\,dS,\qquad f_j=\partial_\nu U_j\big|_{S^2},$$
and the fluxes $f_j$ have mean zero. The boundary pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation. In particular, there are $C,T>0$ depending only on the fixed class such that for $t\ge T$ and $|\xi|\le t$ one can choose null phases with $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=-\xi$, $|\zeta_j|=\sqrt2t$, and obtain the rigorous estimate
$$|\widehat Q(\xi)|\le C\delta e^{Ct}+C\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}t^{-1}N.$$
The factor $\langle\xi\rangle^{1/2}$ is part of this conclusion; this lemma does not assert the sharper stability estimate that would follow from dropping it.

Assume Countable Choice. Write $\langle\xi\rangle=(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}$ and use unitary Fourier transformation on $\mathbb R^3$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $b\ge1$ and $Q\in H^{-1/2}(\mathbb R^3)$,

Consequently, if $t>0$, $L\ge0$ and $a_\xi\in H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^3)$ is any family with $\|a_\xi\|_{H^{1/2}}\le L/t$ for $|\xi|\le b$, its modulated bilinear distributional remainders

$$\left(\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}|R(\xi)|^2\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}\le C\frac{Lb}{t}\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}},$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Indeed the ratio of the two Fourier weights is $\langle\xi\rangle^{-1-2(s-2)}=\langle\xi\rangle^{-2\kappa}$.

For $t\ge\max\{T,b\}$, [F2] gives the pointwise inequality $|\widehat Q(\xi)|\le C\delta e^{Ct}+(C/t)\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}$ for $|\xi|\le b$. The right side is measurable by the nonnegative Fourier integral in [F3]; thus this inequality can be integrated without selecting a measurable family of CGO phases. Square it using $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$, multiply by $\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}$ and integrate. Since $\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}d\xi\le Cb^2$, [F3] yields a low-frequency bound $Cb^2\delta^2 e^{Ct}+Cb^2t^{-2}N^2$, after increasing the exponential constant. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $0<\tau<1$, $0<\rho<1$ and $M>0$. If $q\in H^{1/2+\tau}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ has support in $\overline{B_\rho}$ and norm at most $M$, there are constants $T,C>0$, depending only on $\tau,\rho,M$, such that for every $\zeta\in\mathbb C^3$ with $\zeta\cdot\zeta=0$ and $|\zeta|\ge T$, there is $r_\zeta\in H^2(B_2)$ for which
$$(-\Delta+q)\big(e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r_\zeta)\big)=0\quad\hbox{in }B_2,$$
$$\|r_\zeta\|_{H^{1/2}(B_2)}\le C|\zeta|^{-1}M,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{L^\infty(B_2)}\le C|\zeta|^{-\tau/2}M,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{H^2(B_2)}\le C|\zeta|M(1+M).$$
Here fractional Sobolev norms on the ball are restriction norms from the whole-space Fourier Sobolev spaces. No boundary condition is imposed. The construction is on a larger cube, so the stated regularity holds on a neighborhood of the closed unit ball.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Suppose
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact
set $K_0\subset\Omega$. Let $E_0u$ denote the extension of a representative of
$u$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$, and for $|\alpha|\le k$ let
$E_0(D^\alpha u)$ denote the extension by zero of the corresponding
derivative representative. Then
$$E_0u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad D^\alpha(E_0u)=E_0(D^\alpha u)\quad\text{almost everywhere, }|\alpha|\le k,$$
and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0(D^\alpha u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$. The case
$k=0$ is included, and complex scalars are handled by the same bilinear
pairing.

derivations.claim: Define $J_b(\eta)=\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-1}\,d\xi$. For $|\eta|\ge2b$, $|\eta-\xi|\ge|\eta|/2$ throughout the integration ball, so $\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-1}\le2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$. Polar integration gives $\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}\,d\xi\le Cb^2$ for $b\ge1$. Hence $J_b(\eta)\le Cb^2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$ in this region.

If $|\eta|<2b$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $J_b(\eta)\le(\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-2}\,d\xi)^{1/2}(\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-2}\,d\xi)^{1/2}$. The first integral is at most $Cb$ by polar integration. In the second, the substitution $z=\eta-\xi$ places its domain inside $B_{3b}$, so it is also at most $Cb$. Thus $J_b(\eta)\le Cb$. Since $\langle\eta\rangle\le\sqrt{1+4b^2}\le\sqrt5b$, this is at most $C' b^2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$. Together with step 1.1 this proves $J_b(\eta)\le Cb^2\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}$ for every $\eta$.

Fourier translation gives $\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2=\int\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-1}|\widehat Q(\eta)|^2\,d\eta$. This identity holds for Sobolev distributions as well as smooth functions, because the Fourier transform is represented by a locally square integrable function with the indicated weight, and translation preserves weighted square integrability for every fixed $\xi$. Tonelli [F2] and step 2.1 now give $\int_{|\xi|\le b}\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2\,d\xi=\int|\widehat Q(\eta)|^2J_b(\eta)\,d\eta\le Cb^2\|Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2$.

For the bilinear duality pairing, weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q,a_\xi\rangle|\le\|e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q\|_{H^{-1/2}}\|a_\xi\|_{H^{1/2}}$. The absence of complex conjugation changes the second Fourier factor to its reflection and does not change its Sobolev norm. Squaring, integrating with weight $\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}$, using the bound $L/t$, and applying step 3.1 prove the remainder estimate.
